messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Combat Pilot
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Dizziness): Feeling dizzy or lightheaded, Feeling Ill: Feeling physically unwell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations, Stop Enjoyment: give up pleasant activities, Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
  Threat: Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Negative Appraisals: Emotional Numbness: I feel dead inside, Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Thomas, a 56-year-old European American combat pilot, came to treatment after a long stretch of trying to outrun the aftermath of a life-threatening accident that occurred during a routine flight training mission. He had been handling a high-performance aircraft when a sudden mechanical failure and explosive bang jolted the cockpit; the plane dropped sharply, warning lights flashed, and for a few terrifying moments he was sure he would not get the aircraft back under control. He survived, but in the weeks that followed he found that even ordinary bodily sensations could carry him back to that day. If he felt dizzy or lightheaded on standing, or if he came down with a flu-like sense of feeling physically unwell, his mind immediately went to the cockpit and the brief, sickening loss of control. The same happened with sharp bangs in the environment — a slammed door in the hangar, a backfire from a vehicle, even an unexpected pop on a television program — each sound struck him as though danger were already in the room. In those moments his body became tense and ready to react, and he found himself scanning his surroundings, startled by movement near him as if every quick gesture might signal an emergency.

What unsettled Thomas most was not only the sensations themselves but what they seemed to prove. He had come to believe that the world was dangerous, that the assumptions he had built his life on had been shattered, and that something in him had died that day. He described feeling dead inside, as if the accident had hollowed out the part of him that once felt steady and purposeful. That conviction made the triggering sensations even more ominous: dizziness no longer felt like a passing physical symptom, but like evidence that catastrophe could return at any moment; a bang did not just remind him of the accident, it confirmed his belief that the world could turn lethal without warning. He had always trusted training, procedure, and control, and after the accident he felt those beliefs were completely destroyed. His sense that danger was everywhere made him wary of his own body, and his own numbness seemed to him like proof that he was not the same man who had once flown confidently and lived with a sense of mastery.

Over the months that followed, Thomas began arranging his life around the need to feel safe and in control. He avoided hospitals, ambulances, and physical examinations whenever he could, even when his wife urged him to get checked after minor illnesses. He gave up pleasant activities he used to enjoy, not because he no longer wanted them, but because enjoyment itself felt irresponsible and exposed, as though letting his guard down would invite another disaster. He also began restricting his eating strictly, telling himself that controlling food was one domain in which he could still impose order on a body that had otherwise become unreliable. Yet the more he tried to manage things this way, the more his mind returned to the accident and the more certain he became that the world truly was dangerous. Each avoidance choice seemed to confirm that there was something to fear: if hospitals and examinations were unbearable, maybe there really was a hidden problem in his body; if he had to micromanage food to feel steady, maybe he could not trust himself at all. That inward conclusion deepened his emotional numbness and his shattered beliefs, making it harder to imagine any future that did not revolve around vigilance and loss.

At the same time, those habits kept his body on alert. By narrowing his world, he found himself watching himself more closely, bracing for the next dizzy spell, the next bang, the next sudden movement near him. The effort of staying guarded was exhausting, and the tension never fully left his muscles. He noticed it at work in the flight operations environment, where the noise of equipment, quick motion on the tarmac, and emergency vehicles crossing nearby would jolt him into instant alarm. Instead of easing with familiarity, his alarm made him more determined to avoid medical settings and any situation that might remind him of vulnerability. His wife had begun to notice that he declined dinners, skipped golf with friends, and grew terse whenever someone suggested a checkup. What started as an attempt to protect himself had become a pattern that kept reinforcing the very world he feared: the more he avoided, the more dangerous everything felt, and the more threatening his own reactions became. It was this tightening cycle, along with a recent episode of dizziness that sent him into a panic when he heard an ambulance outside the base clinic, that finally brought him to seek help. Thomas said he was most afraid that he had become permanently trapped in a life of hyperalertness and emotional emptiness, but he was also quietly hoping that treatment might help him feel safe in his own body again and reclaim some sense that the world was not entirely ruined.
